title: First sub-four-minute mile
note: A medical student training in his lunch hour, on a cinder track, in a crosswind, with two friends pacing. 3:59.4, and he was on hospital rounds the next morning.

title: First woman to run Boston
note: Rejected by the race director on the grounds that women were not physiologically capable of it, so she hid in the bushes at the start in her brother's shorts and beat two-thirds of the field.

title: Bib 261
note: Entered as K.V. Switzer, then had the race director try to physically remove her from the course at mile four. Finished, and the photograph did the rest.

title: Marathon at 100
note: Took up running at 89 after losing his wife and son, and finished a marathon at 100 — last in the field, first in the record books, and unable to have it ratified because he had no birth certificate from 1911 Punjab.

title: Sub-three marathon at 72
note: Trained by shuffling in circles round a cemetery near his house for hours at a time, in twenty-year-old shoes. The first man over 70 to break three hours, and it still looks impossible.

title: Marathon at 92
note: A concert pianist who ran her first marathon at 76, survived cancer twice, and set the 90-plus record while being treated for radiation burns on both legs.

title: Ironman at 82
note: The Iron Nun started triathlon at 52 on a priest's suggestion that it would build character, and has finished more than 45 Ironmans. The age group had to be invented for her.
logistics: Entry ~$800 and a body that has been doing this for thirty years

title: Olympic medal at 72
note: Still the oldest Olympic medallist in history, in running deer shooting, having won his first gold at 60. He qualified again at 76 but was too ill to travel.

title: Ran the length of Africa
note: Cape Town to Bizerte: 16,300 km, 352 days, 16 countries, one armed robbery, one visa crisis and a kidney infection. Started as a hungover 20-something in Worthing.

title: A marathon in every country
note: 196 marathons, 196 countries, 674 days, funded by selling his house and promising a dying friend with progeria he would do it.
logistics: 196 visas and about £150k

title: 50 Ironmans, 50 days, 50 states
note: A full-distance triathlon every day for fifty days, driving between states overnight with his family in an RV. Then did 101 consecutive in 2021, because fifty had apparently settled nothing.

title: Man in Motion World Tour
note: 40,000 km in a wheelchair through 34 countries in 26 months — the equivalent of two marathons a day, uphill, on 1980s equipment, with shoulders that were never going to forgive him.

title: Ran across Canada on one leg
note: Finished the coast-to-coast run that Terry Fox could not, 7,924 km over 425 days, also on an above-knee amputation, also at nineteen. The country largely forgot.

title: Ran across Canada dressed as The Flash
note: 5,000 miles unsupported in a superhero suit through a Canadian winter, pulling his kit behind him, after a childhood spent in hospital with a rare spinal condition.

title: Seven ultras in seven days
note: Third instalment: 40 miles a day across seven cities, finishing at Old Trafford before a Rugby League World Cup match. Total raised across the campaigns is now past £8 million.

title: 4,030 pull-ups in 17 hours
note: Third attempt at the record after the first two destroyed his hands and wrists. He also ran a 100-mile race on no training, on broken feet, to qualify for Badwater.

title: First woman to finish the Barkley
note: 59:58:21 — ninety-nine seconds inside the cutoff, on hands and knees at the gate, having also won the 268-mile Spine Race outright in 2019 while expressing milk at checkpoints.

check.factor_why: no course and navigation by map and compass

logistics: You cannot enter the Barkley. It has to let you in.

title: Antarctic crossing, contested
note: 932 miles in 54 days, marketed as the first solo unsupported crossing — a claim the polar community disputes on the grounds that he skied a groomed supply road for the last third.
logistics: Antarctic logistics, six figures

title: South Pole Race, second place
note: 750 km hauling sledges to the Pole against a Norwegian team who had done this sort of thing before. Cracknell got frostbite in his nose; the documentary got the arguments.
logistics: Race entry plus Antarctic support: £70k+

title: Length of Britain, three ways
note: Having swum it in 2013 and cycled it before that, he ran it too — then strung all three together back to back over 51 days for the full set.

title: The James Caird voyage
note: 1,300 km of the Southern Ocean in a 22-foot lifeboat, navigating by four sextant sightings in sixteen days, then a 36-hour unroped traverse of South Georgia's mountains in carpentry boots with screws driven through the soles. Every man survived.

title: Sailed the Pacific in the Snark
note: Built his own boat, could barely navigate, and sailed it from San Francisco to the Solomons anyway — writing all the way, until tropical disease ended the voyage two years in.

title: The River of Doubt
note: Two years after losing the presidency, he descended an uncharted Amazon tributary, cut his leg, developed a fever of 40°C, lost a quarter of his body weight and asked to be left behind. He was not.

title: 33.5 hours awake, alone, over the Atlantic
note: No sleep for 55 hours by the end, no radio, no forward windscreen, hallucinating over the ocean and slapping himself to stay conscious. The endurance problem was the pilot, not the plane.

title: Solo across the Atlantic
note: Just under 15 hours through ice, a cracked manifold and a leaking fuel tank, landing in a field in Derry. Five years to the day after Lindbergh, and she flew it alone too.

title: Mr Universe competitor
note: A milkman and coffin polisher from Fountainbridge who lifted weights three hours a day and competed at Mr Universe before anyone put him in a dinner jacket.

title: Eighth-degree black belt
note: Trained from his army days in Germany onward, founded his own school, and worked karate into the jumpsuit choreography. The rank came from Kang Rhee; the kicks were real.

title: Black belt, Shotokan and hapkido
note: Started at twelve in the Bronx, holds a fifth-dan Shotokan black belt plus capoeira and hapkido training, and did most of the Blade choreography himself.

title: 21 SAS selection, then a broken back
note: Passed reserve special-forces selection, then shattered three vertebrae in a parachute failure in Africa and was told he might not walk unaided. Summited Everest eighteen months later.

title: Raced the 24 Hours of Le Mans
note: Six Olympic cycling golds, then four years of licences and junior series to get an LMP2 seat, and a finish. Different sport, same appetite for suffering in a straight line.

title: Calgary on borrowed sleds
note: Four sprinters from a country with no ice, trained for months, borrowed spare sleds from other teams, and crashed at 130 km/h in the four-man before pushing it across the line.

title: Taekwondo, then cross-country skiing, then taekwondo
note: Qualified for a Winter Games in a sport he had taken up a year earlier, having seen snow perhaps twice, by training on rollerblades and grass in Tonga. Also the flag bearer, also oiled, also in the freezing cold.

title: Kenya's first Winter Olympian
note: A middle-distance runner recruited to cross-country ski, finished last by twenty minutes, and found Bjørn Dæhlie — who had won the gold — waiting at the line for him. Dæhlie later named his son Philip.

title: Olympic halfpipe with no tricks
note: Worked out that qualification rewarded showing up at enough small World Cup events and not falling, so she rode the pipe end to end doing nothing at all, for Hungary, at the Olympics.

title: Big-wall rock climbing
note: Trains and climbs seriously enough to have done multi-pitch routes with professional partners, between albums and film shoots. No competition record, plenty of exposure.

title: Bouldering habit
note: Climbs hard enough to hold his own on real problems and turns up at bouldering gyms unannounced. The physique is a by-product, not the point.

title: The industrial training habit
note: Decades of two-hour sessions, Ashtanga to Gyrotonic to weights, maintained through world tours that are themselves cardio events. Broke a collarbone, three ribs and a hand falling off a horse at 47 and was back on stage that year.
display: Two hours, daily, for thirty years

title: Boston Marathon
note: Seven NASCAR championships and a genuine amateur running habit — he qualified on time rather than on fame, then ran Boston in the rain.

title: BJJ purple belt
note: Trains under a Gracie lineage and has rolled for over a decade — the belt is the kind you cannot buy, whatever the King of Queens résumé suggests.

title: The Murph, on camera
note: Mile, 100 pull-ups, 200 press-ups, 300 squats, mile — done publicly for veterans' charities, in a vest, at a pace that suggested he had done it before.

title: BQ standard, open age group
note: 3:00:00 for men and 3:30:00 for women in the 18-34 band, and even that only gets you into the lottery of cut-offs. The 2026 race tightened the standards by five minutes.
logistics: Qualifying time plus a buffer, at a certified race

title: Sub-1:30 half marathon
note: 4:15/km for 21.1 km — the cleanest single test of whether your marathon ambitions are arithmetic or fantasy.

title: Sub-40 10 km
note: Four minutes a kilometre, ten times. The threshold where club running starts taking you seriously.

title: Sub-20 parkrun
note: The most-attempted barrier in amateur running, free, every Saturday morning, in about 2,000 places.

title: 100 miles inside 24 hours
note: 161 km between one sunrise and the next. The entry qualification for taking ultrarunning seriously, and the point where the sport becomes about digestion and feet.

title: 171 km around Mont Blanc, 46½ hours
note: 10,000 m of climbing through three countries and two nights. The lottery is harder to beat than the cutoff.
logistics: Running Stones, a lottery, and €300

title: 100 miles, 30-hour buckle
note: Squaw Valley to Auburn through canyons that hit 40°C, with a silver buckle for sub-24 and a bronze for sub-30. The oldest 100-miler there is.
logistics: Qualifying race plus a lottery you will lose for years

title: 217 km through Death Valley
note: From 85 m below sea level to the Whitney Portal, in July, on tarmac soft enough to take a shoe print. Invitation only, and the invitation is the easy part.

check.factor_why: a road surface at 50°C in July

logistics: Invitation, a crew of four and a support vehicle

title: Five loops, 60 hours, no course
note: Around 100 miles by the organiser's reckoning and rather more by everyone else's, with 20,000 m of climbing, no markings, and books hidden in the woods to prove you were there. Twenty finishers in forty years.

check.factor_why: no course, no markings and navigation by map and compass

logistics: An application process nobody will explain to you

title: 250 km of Sahara, self-supported
note: Six stages carrying your own food and sleeping bag, with the organisers providing water and a tent. The long stage alone is 80 km.
logistics: €4,000+, a medical certificate and an ECG

title: Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike, Snowdon in 24 hours
note: About 26 km of walking and 3,000 m of ascent, plus 740 km of driving between them, which is the part that actually breaks people.
logistics: A driver who is not also climbing

title: 5,364 m, on foot, in twelve days
note: The most accessible thing on this page with the word Everest in it: a trek, not a climb, but altitude does not care how fit you are at sea level.
logistics: US$1,500-3,000 and twelve days off

title: 4,808 m, the guided classic
note: Two days, a hut, crampons, and roughly 1,500 people a summer. Roped glacier travel, so a guide unless you have the skills yourself.
logistics: Guide ~€1,200 plus hut fees

title: Highest point on every continent
note: Kilimanjaro and Elbrus are treks; Denali and Vinson are expeditions; Everest is Everest. Budget several years and the price of a house.
logistics: US$150,000+ and years of leave

title: Seven channel crossings
note: English, North, Catalina, Molokai, Tsugaru, Gibraltar and Cook Strait — cold, sharks, jellyfish and tides, in whatever order the pilots allow. Fewer than thirty people have all seven.
logistics: Years of pilot bookings and about US$50,000

title: 33 km, usually at night
note: Started at midnight to get the flat water, finished in daylight, with a boat, a kayaker and phosphorescence for company.
logistics: Pilot and observer, ~US$3,500

title: 2.4 km across San Francisco Bay
note: Twenty minutes to an hour in 12-15°C water with a current that will take you to the Golden Gate if you get the ferry angle wrong. The most achievable famous swim there is.
logistics: Organised event entry ~US$200

title: 6.5 km from Asia to Europe
note: The only day of the year the strait closes to shipping. Downstream current, 2,000 swimmers, and a continent change halfway.
logistics: Ballot entry

title: Around Manhattan, 46 km
note: Tidal assistance most of the way, which is the only reason it is possible, plus seven or eight hours in the Hudson and East rivers.
logistics: NYOW entry, qualifying swims, ~US$2,500

title: SwimRun world championship
note: 65 km of running and 10 km of swimming across 26 islands, in a wetsuit and shoes, tethered to a partner the whole way. Pippa Middleton has done it; most people have not heard of it.
logistics: Qualifying race plus a partner who still likes you afterwards

title: 1.5 km / 40 km / 10 km
note: The standard-distance race and the sanest way into the sport. Sub-2:30 is a solid amateur day.

title: 1.9 km / 90 km / 21.1 km
note: Half an Ironman, rather more than half the training. Sub-6 hours is the amateur benchmark.

title: 1,219 km in 90 hours
note: The oldest cycling event still running, older than the Tour. Qualify through a series of brevets, then ride for four days on about six hours of sleep.
logistics: A qualifying brevet series in the same year

who: Land's End to John o' Groats
title: 1,400 km end to end
note: Nine days at touring pace, five if you are pushing, under two if you are chasing the record. The wind decides which.

title: 4,800 km, 12-day cutoff
note: No stages: the clock runs continuously, so the sport is really sleep management. Solo riders average about 90 minutes a night.
logistics: Qualifier, a crew of eight and US$50k

title: A Tour stage, closed roads
note: One mountain stage of that year's Tour, ridden by 15,000 amateurs a week before the professionals, with the same climbs and rather more suffering per kilometre.
logistics: Ballot entry ~€130

title: 200 miles in one ride
note: 322 km, twelve to fifteen hours, and the point at which nutrition, saddle choice and mental state all outrank fitness.

title: 100,000 m of climbing in a year
note: Eleven Everests, spread over twelve months. Roughly 2,000 m a week, which is one proper hilly ride.

title: A mile every day for a year
note: One mile minimum, 365 consecutive days, no exceptions for illness, travel, weather or hangover. The rule is the whole difficulty.

title: A mile every day for 100 days
note: The entry-level version, and the one that actually changes behaviour. Most streaks die in week three.

title: Mile, 100, 200, 300, mile — vested
note: Named for Lt. Michael Murphy, who did it in body armour. Sub-40 in a 20 lb vest is the number people quote; sub-60 unvested is the number most people should.

title: Deadlift twice bodyweight
note: The line between training and lifting. Scales with you, which is why it survives as a benchmark where 500 lb does not.

title: Twenty strict pull-ups
note: Dead hang, no kip, chin over the bar, one set. Roughly the entry standard for military selection courses and out of reach of most gym-goers.

title: 500 kg deadlift
note: Burst blood vessels in his face, passed out on the platform, and said afterwards he thought it might kill him. Nobody had lifted it before; the recovery took months.

title: Marathon pulling a car
note: A 1.4-tonne Mini dragged 42.195 km by harness, in just under twenty hours, on a route that took him past the point where his shoulders stopped being load-bearing.

title: London Marathon at 63
note: A chat-show host of forty years' standing, running his first marathon in his sixties for a charity that funds research into his daughter's condition. Finished it walking-wounded and delighted.

title: Marathons, plural, in his fifties
note: Broadcaster who took up running late, then kept turning up — London, plus a personal habit of running before the breakfast show that predates most of the celebrity running boom.

title: Speed-ramped off a cliff on a motorcycle
note: 13,000 motocross jumps and 500 skydives in preparation, then rode a bike off a Norwegian cliff and base-jumped away from it, six times in one morning, at sixty.
logistics: A film studio's insurance department saying yes

title: A career of doing every stunt himself
note: Fractured skull, dislocated pelvis, broken nose several times over, and no insurance company in Hong Kong would cover him. The outtakes at the end of the films are the injury log.

title: Search-and-rescue pilot
note: Flew genuine mountain rescue missions in his own helicopter while in his fifties and sixties, including hauling a dehydrated hiker off a Wyoming ridge.

title: Competitive carriage driving into his 80s
note: Took up the sport at 50 when his wrists gave out for polo, competed internationally for Britain, and was still driving a four-in-hand at 96.

title: Directing features past 90
note: Lifted weights daily from the 1950s onward and was still doing 14-hour days on set — and riding a horse on camera — at 91. Not a feat with a number, but a rate of decline worth studying.

title: Hill walking and hedge-laying into his 70s
note: Played competitive polo until 57, still walks the Scottish hills in weather that turns back tourists, and lays hedges by hand at Highgrove. Manual labour as a hobby, aristocratic division.

title: Back on the bike six days after open-heart surgery
note: Two valve replacements, one of which went wrong on the table and became emergency open-heart surgery. He was photographed riding again the same week, at 71.

title: The Volvo split, at 52
note: An unedited single take, feet on the mirrors of two reversing lorries, holding a full side split at 52. Karate competitor before he was an actor, and it showed.

title: The perfect ten
note: The scoreboard could not display 10.00 and showed 1.00 instead, because nobody had built it expecting one. She scored seven of them at those Games, at fourteen.

title: Hydrofoiling in a suit, holding a flag
note: A foil board, an American flag and a beer, filmed for the internet. The balance is real even where the framing is absurd.

title: Race-fit at 40 in the hottest cockpit in sport
note: Two hours at 50°C pulling 5g through corners, with a heart rate held near threshold the entire race. Seven titles, and the training load is closer to an endurance athlete's than anyone outside the paddock assumes.

title: Wall of death world record
note: 125 km/h around a vertical wooden wall at 5.2g, held for long enough to grey out. A working lorry mechanic who does this sort of thing on his holidays.

title: Kilimanjaro, then a marathon of concerts
note: One of the Comic Relief Nine on the mountain, then organised the follow-up expeditions. Altitude sickness on the summit push and he kept going.
logistics: Guided trek

title: Summited Kilimanjaro, then nearly died of malaria
note: Reached the top with the Comic Relief group, contracted malaria on the descent, and was hospitalised in intensive care within days of getting home.

title: Carried his brother over the line
note: Gave up a world title to hold up a sibling whose legs had stopped working 700 m from the finish. Professional athletes both, so filed as a reference point rather than a peer — but it belongs in any ledger about what people will do at the edge.

title: The crawl
note: A college student doing the race for a dissertation, leading with 200 m to go, whose legs failed. She crawled, was passed, and crawled across anyway — on live television, which is why the sport exists at the scale it does.

title: Indoor rowing records, set in prison
note: Serving a life sentence for armed robbery when a gym officer put him on an ergometer; he broke British indoor rowing records inside, then became an endurance athlete on release.

title: Nothing here is stranger than the truth
note: A semi-professional baseball player turned cartoonist whose Believe It or Not! syndicated the world's endurance oddities to 80 million readers — the direct ancestor of every list like this one, including this one.
